paragraphs: I was allowed to do a clerkship for one month in March 2024 at the University of Munich in Germany. Life abroad was full of unfamiliar things, but through this study abroad I was able to have valuable and irreplaceable experiences. Here I would like to introduce the content of my clerkship and life there.

The official name of the University of Munich is Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität-München, commonly called LMU. Founded in 1472 by Ludwig IX, it is highly regarded as one of the leading universities in Europe. Every spring, LMU hosts a four-week program called the Winter School in the two fields of neurology and medical oncology, and I took part in the Neurology Winter School (NWS). Exchange students like me gather from countries around the world for this Winter School and learn together in the same program. In particular, exchange students and local LMU students are paired one-to-one, and each pair always acts together and can teach each other. This year there were five NWS exchange students and five local students. My partner was a male fourth-year student who aspires to become a neurologist.

From here I will introduce the content of the clerkship. The daily schedule was fixed in detail in advance, with ward clerkship in the morning and lectures in the afternoon. When I arrived at the ward at 8 a.m., the day began with drawing blood. In Germany it is common for students to do blood draws, line placement and so on, and I too was allowed to draw blood many times. After that, I accompanied the doctors' rounds, and with my partner student took histories, examined patients, wrote in the chart and discussed the necessary tests. In the ward clerkship, each pair was assigned to a different unit and learned there under the guidance of doctors. Our pair was assigned to the general neurology unit, and we could see diverse diseases such as brain tumors, meningitis and ALS. There were also many undiagnosed peripheral neuropathies of unknown cause, and deciding what treatment to give after history taking and examination, considering various viewpoints, was very fresh. Being allowed to do on my own procedures that cannot yet be done in Japan, starting with blood draws, was very exciting. As I repeated them, I steadily improved and gained confidence in the procedures. One female patient looked forward to my coming for the blood draw, and the fact that she was very sad on my last morning is an unforgettable memory. The doctors in my unit were very enthusiastic and kind, and when I asked about diseases and the treatments being given, they taught me in detail. They often took the time during rounds to explain to me. The doctors' meetings and rounds, and history taking with patients, were mostly in German, but there are very many people in Germany who are fluent in English, so not only could I communicate with doctors in English, but I could also enjoy simple conversations with patients. And above all, the presence of my partner student was significant. He explained German conversations in English point by point as they went, so I could keep up with the conversations. I am very grateful to him because I could ask him what I did not understand without hesitation and learn with peace of mind.

After lunch we attended two lectures. They covered all fields, from neurodegenerative diseases to cerebral infarction and case discussions, and every day a specialist gave interesting lectures from the basics to cutting-edge medicine. The one that impressed me most was the lecture on eye movements. I had thought lightly, "Neurology, and today it's the eyes?", but I was deeply impressed to learn that just by looking at eye movements one can infer which place is damaged and how. I was also able to learn various examination methods for looking at eye movements, and I feel I came a step closer to the path of becoming a neurologist. Besides such ward clerkships and lectures, I also had several opportunities to visit outside institutions. For example, I took about two hours to go to a rehabilitation facility in the suburbs, experienced the latest exercise equipment that I had never seen in Japan, and realized the importance of well-equipped facilities and a beautiful environment. I also visited a research institute near the hospital and learned about basic research using mice.

On weekends there were a bus tour of Munich and day trips to Dachau concentration camp and Neuschwanstein Castle. Since all the Winter School students took part, I was able to interact with and become closer to the Oncology students, whom I do not usually have the chance to meet. In this way I feel that the Winter School is a very refined and wonderful program in which not only can you learn something different every day, but pairs help each other and students can interact.

The exchange students were provided with a dormitory about 40 minutes by train from the hospital. It is a student dormitory equipped with a kitchen, tableware and a coin laundry. There was also a supermarket nearby, which was convenient, and I sometimes cooked for myself. Because it is in Olympia Park, I could enjoy walks after school and on holidays. After school I enjoyed going out to eat with my Winter School friends and exploring the city. In Germany, the bread, starting with pretzels, is very delicious, and stopping by a bakery in the morning to eat was one of my pleasures. German cuisine is varied, not only sausages and beer but also dishes I had never seen in Japan, and one can enjoy it for a month without getting bored. The cafeteria, where the menu changes every day, is also recommended. As for sightseeing too, there are abundant attractive places such as churches and markets, and there are many parks with beautiful ponds and trees where you can feel nature. I also went to watch ballet and to the theater. Munich has good public safety, and I truly feel glad I was able to study abroad here. I also went a little further to towns in southern Germany and sightseeing to Prague and Vienna.

As for the differences between Germany and Japan that I felt through this study abroad, first of all, foreign students were very proactive. Interrupting the doctor's talk during a lecture to ask a question oneself is quite normal, and in the ward clerkship too I saw scenes in which they put forward their opinions about a patient's treatment plan, saying they think this way is better. When I asked them, they replied that if you ask right away about a point you wonder about, you yourself will be convinced and that it is only natural, and I remember being very impressed. I learned the importance of expressing one's will without being too reserved, and I try to put it into practice in Japan too. Also, unlike Japan, Germany has as many as three big tests like the national exam, and they start even before entering the clinical clerkship. For that reason the amount of knowledge of medical students is considerably higher than I imagined, and in fact I was taught by my fourth-year partner student many times. They could also do procedures such as blood draws quite well, so they looked very reliable and it stimulated me to try harder. Regarding neurology, there was no great difference from Japan in the content from examination to treatment, but, for example, it was shocking that lumbar puncture is performed with the patient seated and without local anesthesia. In the hospital rooms there were no partition curtains between patients, and seeing them chatting casually, I felt it was a cultural difference.

This study abroad was not only my first study abroad but also my first time living alone and traveling alone. Before going I could not imagine what kind of life awaited me and was full of anxiety, but now that I have finished safely, I am filled with a great sense of accomplishment. From the preparation and procedures for study abroad it was hard because I did not know what was needed, and of course after arriving I had to think about everything myself and take action on my own. Because of the language problem, I sometimes could not get my meaning across and felt frustrated and pained. There were also countless troubles that made me panic and want to cry, such as my smartphone SIM breaking, losing important things, and trains being delayed so that I doubted I could get there. At such times I asked myself what was the best course of action and what I wanted to do, thought it through, and became able to actually act on it, and when I recall how I was before, I feel I have grown a great deal. There were also companions who always helped me, worried together, and found solutions. The companions I was able to meet here are a very, very big treasure for me.

Finally, I would like to express my deep gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office who gave me this wonderful opportunity, and to the doctors of LMU and everyone concerned who looked after me during my study abroad. In addition, my gratitude is endless to all the students who supported me locally and to my family and friends who cheered me on in Japan. Thank you very much.
